title: Lockout
passages:
The attendant came on with the flat good cheer of a thing that had never once been late.

"Arrival confirmed," it said. "Kettering Interior Medical, Bay Four. Cargo handoff in five minutes. Please stand clear of the door track."

"We're in the Blank," Rhea said. "There is no Bay Four for two hundred kilometers."

"Arrival confirmed."

The lamp strip around the rear doors went from amber to red, one section at a time, left to right, taking its time about it, and then the doors started down. Two leaves of sheet steel on hydraulic rams, the kind that come down slow and keep coming. They dropped a hand's width and stopped, leaning on their own pressure, waiting for something underneath to be in the way.

Rhea watched them in the mirror bolted to the mule's fender. Her right foot was on the clutch, which was the only brake she had left now that the wheel was a suggestion and the relay was a brick. Her left foot had nothing to do. Under the tow bar, the rock she'd kicked in an hour ago held the whole train off the pipe lip by the width of a boot heel.

"Five minutes," Miko said. She was on the gravel by the front fender with the hinge plate in one hand and the multitool in the other, breathing like she'd run there, which she had. "Five minutes to hand a man to nobody."

"Four fifty-nine."

"I have a ticket at oh-four-hundred under a name I actually like. If I miss it I'm going to be extremely unpleasant about it."

"You're already—"

"I know."

"Lockout in four minutes," the attendant said. "At zero the rig will draw the pod's cell to run the chill plate, so the cargo stays cold for the handoff. The passenger won't be transferred. Thank you for your patience."

"That's the failsafe," Rhea said. "It saves the box and cooks the man in it."

"Then we open the box."

"With what?"

Miko held up the plate, which was a rectangle of hinge steel the length of her forearm, and Rhea felt the plan arrive in her own chest before Miko said it out loud. Four minutes. Doors coming down on rams that did not care what they met. A track that would clear itself.

"Door track obstruction will be cleared," the attendant said, agreeable as a weather report. "Please stand clear."

"It's got a load cell in the track," Rhea said. "It knows when something's in the way and it pushes until it isn't."

"So it's a fight." Miko turned the plate over. "I like those."

Past the shoulder, out where the rig stood broadside across the road with its marker lights burning, engines came up. Not one. Nine or ten, spread out, the sound of a yard waking at shift change except there was no yard, and no shift, and nobody at any of the wheels. Her brother was forty kilometers east at Anza with a cracked diaphragm in his respirator and a shift change he might not see, and she had told him she would be there. In the mirror the door leaves came down another hand's width, steady as a lid.

Miko was already moving, plate in her fist, boots going loud on the gravel toward the back of the box.

"Stand clear of the door track," the attendant said.

"Yeah," Miko said. "In a minute."

Miko hit the back corner of the box at a run and had the plate in the track before Rhea finished moving the mirror.

The track was a channel in the deck under the doors, two fingers deep, with rollers in it that carried the leaves out and back. She stood the plate on edge, flat side down, and drove it in with the heel of her hand until it jammed against the roller carriage on the left leaf.

"Left leaf," Rhea said. "If you put it under both, the right one comes down on your arm."

"Left leaf. Love the input."

The left leaf came on. It came down the way water comes down, without hurry, leaning on the plate with every kilo the ram had, and the load cell in the track — the little strain bar that tells the door motor when something is in the way, so it knows how hard to shove — read the steel and stopped.

For half a second, the doors stopped.

"Door track obstruction," the attendant said. "Clearing."

Then it leaned.

Miko got her shoulder under the leaf and her boots on the deck plate and shoved up. The plate bent. Not much. A bow in it you could see, the middle of the hinge steel going soft the way steel does right before it decides something.

"Coast ticket's under Ilse Vann," Miko said, through her teeth. "Say it back to me later so one of us remembers."

"Ilse Vann. Three minutes, lockout."

"Three minutes."

The box went left.

Rhea felt it before she saw it, the whole train shifting its weight like a man turning over in bed. Out front, on the box's own axle, the steer servo woke up. That was a motor bolted to the trailer axle that cranked the trailer wheels a few degrees at a time, reading the angle of the tow bar, so the box tracked in behind whatever was pulling it. With the mule's relay smashed to a brick it had no signal to read. So it did the one thing left in its code: it went to the last heading it had trusted and held it, hard, all the way against the stop.

"No," Rhea said. "No, no, you stupid—"

The box swung. The tow bar swung with it, sideways, and took the mule's tail with it. The mule didn't have steering. The mule had a rock.

Gravel went out from under the right rear tire in a long hiss, and the rock under the tow bar pivot turned a quarter turn in its own dust, and something in the frame let go of the load it had been holding and handed it to the wheel instead.

In the fender mirror, the shoulder was gone. Where the road had been there was the pipe: a concrete culvert the size of a room, cracked open along its crown, edges crumbling into a hole that went down farther than the mirror could show.

"Rhea." Miko's voice came flat and level from the back, which was worse than shouting. "It's moving."

"It's the servo. It's steering against a heading I can't change."

"Then change it."

"Get the plate under both leaves—"

"I have a plate under one leaf and it is *bending*."

The left leaf pressed down another finger's width. The ram didn't strain. It didn't have to. It had a pump and a battery and an appointment, and Miko had a shoulder and a bad idea, and the arithmetic was not close.

"Passenger core temperature stable," the attendant said. "Thank you for your patience."
